title: Can we prove God? (ST I.2)
hook: Thomas thinks reason can reach God's existence, though not everything about God

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace perfects nature: God's gift finishes what we are. Your line was grace completes.

Fresh snow, early morning, and a line of small prints crosses the yard, under the fence, and away. Nobody saw the fox. Tracks don't make themselves. You can know something passed, even its size and its hurry, without ever seeing its face. Now ask a question Thomas Aquinas asks near the start of the Summa. Can a person, thinking hard and honestly, get to God by reason? Or only by faith? Thomas's answer is neither of the easy ones. Today's word is the question itself.
screen: `PRINTS IN THE SNOW.` → `NOBODY SAW THE FOX.` → `CAN REASON GET TO GOD?`

segments.voice: Thomas takes it in steps. First: is God's existence obvious? In itself, yes, but not to us. His evidence is a psalm: the fool says in his heart, there is no God. If a person can think the opposite, it isn't obvious to us. Second: can it be shown, then? Yes, but only one way: from effects. We can't start from what God is, because we don't see that. We start from the world and reason back to its cause, the way you reason from tracks to the fox. Here he leans on Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Now the limits. Reason can reach that God is, not everything about God. Later in the Summa, Thomas says God being three persons, Father, Son and Spirit, is known by revelation, not by natural reason. And in the very first article he says something humbling: even the truths about God that reason can reach would be known only by a few, after a long time, with many errors mixed in. That's why, he says, God revealed them too. One more kindness. God's existence, Thomas says, isn't strictly an article of faith but something faith builds on, the way grace builds on nature. Yet a person who can't follow a proof may simply hold it by faith. No one is shut out for not being a philosopher. So the answer is yes, and. Reason can reach. It just doesn't reach the end of God.
screen: `OBVIOUS IN ITSELF, NOT TO US.` · `SHOWN FROM EFFECTS, LIKE TRACKS.` · `THAT GOD IS, NOT ALL GOD IS.` · `NO ONE SHUT OUT FOR LACK OF PROOFS.` · then, large: `BEING UNDERSTOOD BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question you care about and usually rush past, about God or a choice in front of you, and say it in one plain sentence. Then sort, slowly, what you actually know, what you're only assuming, and what you'd need to find out, without deciding the answer yet. If you pray, hand the question to God at the end.
Can we prove God? Thomas's answer: reason can show that God is, working back from the world, though it can't reach everything about God.
Your line: reason can reach. That closes a week, from the Our Father to a boy in a tower. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that God's existence can be known by natural reason from created things, and Catholic schools and universities often teach Thomas's arguments alongside the Church's teaching on revelation.
